pages.title: The Lady Knowledge Labs home lab
pages.summary: Abstract. Lady Knowledge Labs runs a small private computing lab in a residence: one virtualization host, two bare-metal servers (one for the Kubernetes control plane, one for infrastructure services), a network storage array, and a residential internet connection. We use it to build and prove infrastructure designs before we propose them at work, and to run a modest set of research tools for colleagues. This page describes what the lab is for, the constraints it operates under, the principles that shape it, and its architecture in a single pass. The articles listed at the end each take one subsystem and tell its story in full: what we built, what broke, and what we changed as a result.
pages.text:
What the lab is, and why it exists The lab is a proving ground for our work in university IT. Designs for that work (container orchestration, identity governance, batch computing) are built here first, run under real load, and broken here first. A design that reaches a proposal has already met real hardware, real users, and its own failure modes. That purpose sets the bar. A lab that only demonstrates a happy path teaches little. This one is expected to carry real workloads for real people, to be rebuilt from its repository, and to record its own failures. Three kinds of work run on it: Platform experiments. A Kubernetes cluster that serves as the prototype for a campus container platform's successor, an identity stack that federates a directory with a university single sign-on service, and a small batch-computing cluster for staging scheduler designs. Research tools for colleagues. Collaborative LaTeX editing, Jupyter notebooks, access to language models through a single gateway, and a read-only view of the cluster. Colleagues sign in with their university accounts, and every request for access is reviewed by hand. Household services. A media server and a few personal applications. They matter here because they have daily users and no tolerance for data loss, and it was their data that exposed the storage and backup failures described below. The lab is young. Its repository began in April 2026 and held more than six hundred commits when this page was written. The configuration behind everything described here lives in that repository. Constraints The lab's design is mostly a response to its constraints. They are listed first because nearly every decision in the articles traces back to one of them. One hypervisor. Every virtual machine runs on a single Proxmox host, including the database server and the Kubernetes workers. There is no live migration and no high availability at the virtualization layer. Losing that host means rebuilding everything it ran, so the rebuild path has to be written down, automated, and recoverable from backups kept somewhere else. Older silicon. The hypervisor's processor is an Intel Ivy Bridge part, which supports the x86-64-v2 instruction set but not v3. Some upstream projects now build their enterprise Linux packages for v3, and those binaries refuse to start on this host. We build some tools from source and take others from the distribution's own repositories instead of the vendor's. Production fleets contain old hardware too, and a design that silently assumes the newest instruction set has a dependency nobody wrote down. One bare-metal control plane. The Kubernetes control plane runs on a single physical machine, separate from the hypervisor, so the control plane's machine is not lost with the hypervisor. The cluster's state lives in the database, which is a virtual machine, so after a hypervisor loss the cluster is rebuilt by restoring that database and reprovisioning the workers. A multi-node control plane is deliberately deferred. Shared storage over the network. Virtual machine disks and Kubernetes block volumes live on a Synology storage array reached over iSCSI. Some software, etcd and SQLite among them, tolerates network storage poorly. A residential network. The lab sits behind a home internet connection and a home router, and most of its public names resolve to that connection; this site's own host sits behind a proxy instead. Public services must be reachable without exposing the lab's interior. An operator behind a full-tunnel VPN. The operator's workstation often runs a university VPN that sends all traffic through the campus network, including traffic meant for the lab in the next room. Administration therefore cannot assume a local path to the lab. It has to work over a path the VPN does not capture. One operator. There is no second administrator to remember how something works. Anything that exists only in one person's memory is, for practical purposes, already lost. Principles Three principles follow from those constraints. Each is reflected in how the repository is built. Everything as code Virtual machines are provisioned by Terraform driving Foreman, which installs the operating system over the network. Ansible configures every managed host and deploys most cluster workloads; the repository holds 16 Helm charts. Argo CD tracks a small set of charts that Ansible does not deploy, with manual sync, so drift becomes visible before anything reconciles it. Significant decisions are recorded as architecture decision records, fifteen so far, each stating the context and the alternatives that were rejected. The reason is the single operator. A lab that can be rebuilt from its repository survives both the loss of its hardware and the fading of its operator's memory. A lab configured by hand survives neither. Identity first Colleague-facing services authenticate through one identity layer, and are designed so that access to them is granted through a governance process rather than by editing a service directly. Some operator tools still use their own local logins. A directory is the authority for the lab's own accounts. Keycloak federates that directory and brokers university single sign-on, so a colleague signs in with an account they already have. midPoint holds the access model: who may use which tool, which grants need approval, and which roles imply which group memberships. Putting identity first means a new service begins by deciding who may use it and how that decision is reviewed. It does not begin by creating local accounts. Recovery designed in Every stateful component is meant to have a named backup mechanism and a place in a written restore order. Secrets are split into tiers; the keys and recovery material that open them are kept in an encrypted bundle outside the lab; and the cluster's own state lives in a database that is archived continuously. A job reporting success is not evidence that a backup holds what it should: the lab once had a backup job that succeeded every night while protecting none of the data it was meant to protect. The per-application backup jobs that replaced it fail when a database copy they captured is missing from the snapshot, or, for the one job that dumps a database server, when the dump is implausibly small. The architecture in one pass This section walks the lab from the outside in: how a request arrives, where it is served, how the caller is identified, where state lives, and how that state is protected. One runs the Kubernetes control plane; it moved there from a virtual machine in May 2026. The other is the infrastructure server: it runs provisioning, the internal certificate authority, HashiCorp Vault, and DNS, and it is the first machine rebuilt in the written restore order. An operator workstation with a GPU serves the local language models behind the model gateway. The cluster is RKE2 with Cilium for networking, and MetalLB announces service addresses on the local network. Rancher, which manages the cluster, runs inside it, so there is one cluster to operate and back up rather than two. The cluster's datastore is the decision with the most history behind it, and the lab's first serious failure. RKE2 ships with embedded etcd, and etcd needs storage that commits writes quickly. The lab's virtual disks first sat on a single local SATA disk, where under control-plane load etcd requests took as long as thirty seconds, with reads queued behind commits waiting on the disk; the RKE2 server could not renew its leader-election lease and restarted roughly every seventy-five seconds. Moving the virtual disks to the iSCSI array, together with turning off a source of heavy watch traffic, ended the crash loop, but under a heavy installation etcd's request durations still peaked at several seconds, far above etcd's guidance. Our decision record judged that margin too thin to build on, and in May 2026 we replaced embedded etcd with kine, a shim that serves the etcd API from a SQL database, backed by the lab's PostgreSQL server. A small set of configuration secrets, including the credential Ansible uses to reach Vault, are encrypted with Ansible Vault. Service credentials and values that rotate live in HashiCorp Vault, which keeps its state in cloud object storage and unseals itself through a cloud key-management service, so a restart needs no person holding unseal keys. The keys that open the first two tiers, and Vault's own recovery material, are kept in an encrypted break-glass bundle stored outside the lab. Data and storage One PostgreSQL 16 server is the lab's shared database. It holds the cluster's datastore, the identity service's database, and the databases of many cluster applications, each as a separate tenant. A single database server is a single point of failure, and we accept that at this scale. It is protected by continuous WAL archiving and scheduled full and differential backups with pgBackRest, which we build from source because the vendor's packages require the newer instruction set. Bulk files live on an NFS gateway in front of the storage array. Application databases no longer do. In June 2026 we moved application configuration volumes from NFS to iSCSI block volumes provisioned through the Synology CSI driver, after SQLite databases on network file storage proved to be the cause of repeated application stalls and restarts. Host file systems and most application volumes are backed up with restic. Both restic and pgBackRest write to Backblaze B2, encrypted by the client before upload, with the provider's server-side encryption enabled as well. Observability Prometheus collects host and service metrics, and Alertmanager delivers alerts to a phone through a self-hosted ntfy server, so alerting needs no outside mail relay. Since September 2026 a self-hosted SigNoz instance has also collected telemetry from AI coding-agent sessions, alongside host metrics. For instrumented sessions it shows where agent work is happening. A session reports only if it started after telemetry was configured, and sessions from one of the two agent tools can be placed by machine and time but not by project. Reaching the lab from elsewhere The operator administers the lab through a bastion host joined to a Tailscale network. Tailscale's encrypted tunnels travel over the public internet as ordinary traffic, so the university VPN's full tunnel does not capture them. This path has been in service since August 2026. Failures that shaped the design The datastore failure is told above, under Compute. Two more failures changed the design, and the articles tell both in full. The sign-in that failed forever. In August 2026, brokered university sign-ins by people who also held a directory account failed in realms that federated the directory read-only. On every brokered sign-in, Keycloak updates the user's profile from the incoming assertion. The university supplies a first name in a different form from the directory's, so Keycloak tried to write the change to a read-only directory, threw an error, and abandoned the sign-in before saving the account link. Every retry started over. The committed change sets the federation's edit mode to UNSYNCED : Keycloak may now edit its local copy of the user, and it still never writes to the directory. The backup that protected nothing. When application configuration moved from NFS to block volumes in June 2026, the host-level backup kept running and kept succeeding, but it was backing up the abandoned copies left on NFS. For nearly two months, thirteen volumes of live data had no backup, while the documentation said they did. On 1 August 2026 we added a backup job per application that runs beside the volume it protects, and made each file-level job fail if a database copy it captured is missing from its snapshot; the one job that dumps a database server fails if the dump is implausibly small. The backup failure gave no signal at all, and the sign-in failure surfaced only as a generic error to the person signing in. Each fix moved the lab toward designs that fail instead of reporting success, or that cannot fail that way at all. Reading guide The articles below are written to stand alone. Each opens with an abstract, follows the same arc (context, constraints, design, what went wrong, what we learned, current state), and ends with references. Kubernetes on PostgreSQL . The datastore chronology: an etcd crash loop on local SATA, iSCSI and less watch traffic ending it with little margin, then kine on a continuously archived PostgreSQL, authenticated by client certificates over mutual TLS. Start here if you run Kubernetes on modest or shared storage. Identity as the spine . Directory federation, a hub realm, brokering university SAML, and governance with approvals in midPoint, including the read-only federation setting that broke brokered sign-in for people who also held a directory account, and what UNSYNCED changes. Secrets in three tiers . SOPS at provisioning, Ansible Vault for configuration, HashiCorp Vault at runtime with KMS auto-unseal; what recovery keys can and cannot do, and why the break-glass bundle is kept outside the lab. Backups that restore . restic and pgBackRest to object storage, how a move to block storage silently orphaned application backups for nearly two months, and the rule it produced: each per-application backup job fails when a database copy it captured is missing from its snapshot, or, for a database-server dump, when the dump is implausibly small. Later releases will cover the public edge, storage, reaching a lab from behind a full-tunnel VPN, certificate management, observability for AI agents, and documentation treated as a product. References Upstream documentation for the components whose behavior this page relies on: kine, the etcd API over SQL: https://github.com/k3s-io/kine RKE2 external datastores: https://docs.rke2.io/datastore/external Keycloak Server Administration Guide, LDAP and Active Directory federation, including edit modes: https://www.keycloak.org/docs/latest/server_admin/index.html midPoint documentation: https://docs.evolveum.com/midpoint/ HashiCorp Vault, AWS KMS seal: https://developer.hashicorp.com/vault/docs/configuration/seal/awskms SOPS: https://github.com/getsops/sops Ansible Vault guide: https://docs.ansible.com/ansible/latest/vault_guide/index.html pgBackRest user guide: https://pgbackrest.org/user-guide.html restic documentation: https://restic.readthedocs.io/en/stable/ Let's Encrypt challenge types, including DNS-01: https://letsencrypt.org/docs/challenge-types/ Traefik ACME certificate resolvers: https://doc.traefik.io/traefik/https/acme/ MetalLB: https://metallb.io/ Cilium: https://docs.cilium.io/en/stable/ Tailscale: https://tailscale.com/kb/1151/what-is-tailscale The design reasoning on this page comes from the lab's own architecture decision records, which are not published. These include ADR-001 (kine on PostgreSQL instead of embedded etcd), ADR-002 (three-tier secrets), ADR-003 (B2 server-side encryption), ADR-004 and ADR-005 (building for x86-64-v2), and ADR-014 (university SAML broker identity mapping).

pages.title: Backups that restore
pages.summary: Abstract. The backups this article describes go off-site to Backblaze B2 through two tools. pgBackRest protects the shared PostgreSQL server with continuous WAL archiving and scheduled full and differential backups. restic protects host file systems and, through jobs that run inside the Kubernetes cluster, application data on block storage for the services that have backup jobs. Both encrypt their repositories on the client before anything leaves the lab. This article describes that design and the failure that reshaped it. In June 2026 we moved application configuration volumes from NFS to iSCSI block volumes. The host-level restic job could not see the new volumes, so it went on backing up the copies left behind on NFS, and it reported success every night. For nearly two months the live data had no backup, while our own documentation said it did. The jobs we added on 1 August 2026 nearly repeated the mistake: their first version produced backups that contained no databases and still succeeded, and only a restore exposed it. The rule that came out of it is a per-job dump assertion. The file-level jobs count the database copies in each new snapshot and fail, before pruning anything, if any database the dump step captured is missing; the one job that dumps a database server fails if its dump is implausibly small.
pages.text:
This is one article in a series. The overview describes the lab as a whole and the constraints it works under. Context The lab runs on one hypervisor, beside a network storage array and a few bare-metal servers. Losing the hypervisor means rebuilding everything it ran, and losing the storage array means losing every virtual disk and block volume on it. A backup kept inside the lab protects against neither, so the backups this article describes are written to object storage outside it. Two kinds of state need protecting, and they need different tools. The first is the shared PostgreSQL server. It holds the Kubernetes cluster's datastore, the identity service's database, and the databases of many cluster applications, each as a separate tenant. Copying the files of a database that is being written to is at best a best-effort backup, and the cluster's datastore changes constantly, so it needs a tool that understands PostgreSQL's write-ahead log. The second is everything else: configuration and state on host file systems, user files on the NFS gateway, and the configuration volumes of applications running in the cluster. Much of that last group is small SQLite databases, which carry a household's history (what was watched, what was saved, how each service is set up) and cannot be downloaded again. Constraints Off-site by default. The lab has one of everything that matters, so a backup that stays in the lab shares the fate of what it protects. Encrypted before it leaves. The object store should see only ciphertext, encrypted with keys the operator holds. Older silicon. The hypervisor supports the x86-64-v2 instruction set but not v3. The PostgreSQL project's own pgBackRest packages are compiled for v3 and will not start on it. Block volumes with no snapshots. The storage array's CSI driver, as deployed, ships without snapshot support, so the cluster cannot take a volume snapshot and back up a clone of it. Volumes attach to one node. Application volumes are read-write-once: each is attached to the node that runs its application, and to no other. One operator. There is no second person to notice a backup that quietly stops protecting anything. Left alone, such a backup is found when someone needs it. The credentials each tool uses are read from HashiCorp Vault when Ansible configures the host or deploys the chart, as the secrets article describes. PostgreSQL: pgBackRest pgBackRest runs on the database server. PostgreSQL hands each completed WAL segment to pgBackRest, which pushes it to the object store asynchronously from a local spool, with four parallel processes. A full backup runs every Sunday and a differential backup runs on each of the other six days. Uploads are compressed with zstd and encrypted with AES-256-CBC under a cipher passphrase held in Vault. Retention keeps two full backups and seven differentials, and WAL is kept back to the oldest full backup that remains, so the repository supports point-in-time recovery across that window. A single pgBackRest stanza covers the whole PostgreSQL cluster. Because every tenant lives on one server, one restore brings back every tenant database at once, including the Kubernetes datastore. Two details come from the constraints. We build pgBackRest from source, pinned to a release, because the PostgreSQL project's binary needs an instruction set our hardware lacks; our decision record (ADR-004) found no x86-64-v2 build in that repository, and EPEL does not package pgBackRest at all. And the Ansible role runs pgbackrest check after creating the stanza, which fails unless PostgreSQL's WAL is actually reaching the repository, so a configuration that looks right but archives nothing does not pass that step. Host file systems: restic Three hosts run a restic client installed by an Ansible role: the infrastructure server, the NFS gateway, and the database server, where file-level backup is a coarse safety net beside pgBackRest. Each host writes to its own restic repository, so one host's backups and locks never touch another's. A systemd timer runs the backup daily, and a second timer is scheduled weekly to forget and prune old snapshots. Retention keeps the last 3 snapshots and 24 hourly, 14 daily, 4 weekly, 12 monthly and 3 yearly snapshots. What goes into each backup is chosen per host, and so is what stays out. The largest exclusion is the media library on the NFS gateway, many terabytes that can be downloaded or ripped again. User content beside it, such as music, photos and books, is kept. Application data on block storage: one job per application Application configuration volumes live on iSCSI block storage, which no host-level backup can see. For the services that have backup jobs, they are backed up by restic running inside the cluster, as one Kubernetes CronJob per application, defined in the same Helm chart that deploys those applications. Each job mounts its application's volume directly. Because the volume is read-write-once and already attached to the application's node, the job carries a required pod-affinity rule that places it on the same node as the application. We confirmed both ways that without the rule, the scheduler can place the job elsewhere, and the pod then fails to attach the volume. With no volume snapshots available, mounting the live volume beside the running application is the only way in, which makes the next rule essential. Live databases are never copied as files. An init container runs SQLite's online backup API against each database, read-only, and writes a consistent copy to a scratch volume. restic then backs up that copy together with the rest of the volume, and the raw database files and their write-ahead logs are excluded from the file sweep. The online backup copies pages, so it works even for an application that ships its own SQLite build with custom collations. Where a job discovers databases by name rather than from a list, a file named like a database that turns out not to be SQLite is copied as-is instead of failing the job. One application keeps its data in a MariaDB server instead of SQLite, and its job takes a logical dump over the network in a single transaction, because copying a running InnoDB data directory file by file is not crash-safe. Each application has its own repository , as each host does, so the jobs never contend for a repository lock. They use the same credentials as the host backups and keep the last 3 snapshots and 14 daily, 4 weekly, 12 monthly and 3 yearly snapshots. They run daily, after the host-level run, so the object store is not written by both at once. If the cluster was down at the scheduled time, a job still runs if the cluster comes back within two hours, instead of skipping the day. What is kept follows one rule: back up what is irreplaceable. Anything a rescan or a download regenerates is excluded, however long regenerating it would take. For the media server, that took the configuration volume from about 125 GB, mostly generated thumbnails, transcodes and downloaded metadata, to well under one gigabyte: its library database, its preferences, and little else. The dump step fails the job outright if a database it was told to capture is missing, or if any database it finds cannot be captured. It then records how many databases it captured. After the upload, the restic step counts the database copies in the new snapshot. If fewer are present than the dump step recorded, the job fails, and it fails before it prunes, so the previous good snapshot is kept. The MariaDB job takes a different form of the same check: it refuses a dump of a kilobyte or less, since a server that answers but returns nothing useful would otherwise produce a backup that looks complete. The rule exists because of the two failures that follow. What went wrong The backup that protected nothing Until June 2026, application configuration lived on NFS, and from late May the NFS gateway's restic job captured it every night. The SQLite databases on those volumes were the cause of repeated application stalls and restarts, because NFS locking does not suit SQLite. Between 7 and 19 June we moved the configuration volumes to iSCSI block volumes provisioned through the storage array's CSI driver. The host-level backup did not follow. It backs up paths on the NFS gateway, and the live data was no longer there. The job went on backing up the copies the migration had left behind, which no longer changed, and it reported success every night. Thirteen volumes were affected. On 1 August 2026 the job was still capturing copies about eight weeks old. For one application, the newest database in the backup was dated 7 June, while the live database was dated 30 July. The documentation made it worse. Our backup plan still said this data was covered. Had we needed it, we would have found the gap in the middle of a restore. The fix that backed up no databases On 1 August we added the per-application jobs. The first version excluded raw database files with an unanchored pattern, matching any file whose name ends in .db . That pattern also matched the consistent copies the dump step had just written. The jobs reported success and stored backups that held no databases at all. The job's success said nothing about it. A restore did: the first restore test from the object store reported that it had restored a single item of zero bytes. We anchored the exclusions to the application's live volume, so that they can no longer match the dump directory. Then we added the snapshot count described above, so that a file-level job cannot report success when a database it captured is missing from the snapshot. The check needed debugging of its own. Its first version listed only the top of the dump directory, so it counted zero for applications whose databases sit in subdirectories, and it failed backups that were good. It now counts across the whole snapshot listing. After those changes, all twelve jobs completed with their checks satisfied. We then restored one application from the object store into a fresh pod. SQLite's integrity check passed, and the restored database held the same record counts as the live one. A tool that would not start The pgBackRest role began with the vendor's package. On the hypervisor's older processor, every invocation of that binary exited at once, reporting that the CPU's instruction-set level was lower than required. The project's repository had no build for that level, and EPEL did not package pgBackRest. The role now builds a pinned release from source with the system compiler and installs it beside the system's own binaries, and every task and timer calls it by its absolute path. The first full backup with the source-built binary completed the same evening, 11 May 2026. What we learned A job's success is a claim about the job, not about the data. The host backup succeeded for eight weeks while protecting none of the data it was meant to protect, and the first replacement succeeded while storing no databases. In both cases every signal we had said all was well. The per-job assertion moves the check from "did the command exit cleanly" to "is the thing we care about in the snapshot", and it is placed so that a failure keeps the last good snapshot instead of pruning toward a bad one. Moving data is a backup change. The migration in June was a storage change, made for good reasons. None of the commits that made it mentions backups, and the backup was defined by paths on another machine. The new jobs live in the same Helm chart as the volumes they protect, so the backup of each volume is defined next to the volume itself. Documentation is a claim, too. The backup plan said the data was covered. It had not been updated when the data moved. A statement of coverage needs the same scrutiny as the configuration it describes. A restore found what the job could not. The empty backups were found by restoring, not by reading logs or counting snapshots, and we restored once more before trusting the fix. The per-job assertion now catches the specific failure that restore found: a snapshot missing a database the dump step captured. It does not prove that any other part of a snapshot will restore. The check is code, and code has bugs. The first version of the assertion failed good backups. A check that is wrong in that direction is noisy rather than dangerous, but it is still wrong, and it had to be tested against real backups like everything else. Current state The shared PostgreSQL server is protected by pgBackRest 2.58.0, built from source, with continuous asynchronous WAL archiving, a full backup every Sunday and a differential backup on the other six days, keeping two full backups and seven differentials. One stanza covers every tenant database. Host file systems on the infrastructure server, the NFS gateway and the database server are configured for daily restic backups, one repository per host, with a weekly prune timer. Application data on block storage for the services that have backup jobs is backed up by twelve CronJobs configured in the cluster, using restic 0.19.1: eleven file-level jobs, one per application volume, and one logical database dump. Each file-level job dumps its SQLite databases through the online backup API and fails before pruning unless the new snapshot contains every database the dump step captured. The database-dump job fails on a dump of a kilobyte or less. The rule described here belongs to these twelve jobs, as the commit of 1 August 2026 introduced them. Every backup this article describes is written to Backblaze B2, outside the lab, into a restic or pgBackRest repository encrypted on the client. pages.title: Identity as the spine
pages.summary: Abstract. The lab's colleague-facing services sign people in through one identity layer, and are designed so that access to them is granted through a governance process rather than by editing a service. Some operator tools still use their own local logins. Three products divide the work. An Active Directory domain is the authority for the lab's own accounts. Keycloak federates that directory, brokers the university's SAML identity provider, and issues the tokens services trust. midPoint holds the access model: which applications exist, which roles grant access to them, and which grants need a person's approval. This article describes that design. It then tells the failures that shaped it. The most instructive was a read-only directory setting that, for two weeks in August 2026, made every brokered sign-in by a person whose directory account carried a different first name fail on every retry, and what the UNSYNCED edit mode changes: Keycloak may edit its own copy of the user and still never writes to the directory.
pages.text:
This is one article in a series. The overview describes the lab as a whole and the constraints it works under. Context The lab's users come from two places. Lab accounts, the operator's among them, live in the lab's directory. Colleagues live at the university, which runs its own single sign-on service on Shibboleth; they have no account in the lab's directory and should not need one. Keycloak serves OpenID Connect and SAML to the lab's services. It organizes users, clients and identity sources into realms. The lab's realms grew one application at a time, and most of them carry their own copy of the directory federation. As colleagues began to sign in, each realm that admitted them also needed its own connection to the university, so the same identity sources were being configured again and again. The lab is also where we try identity-governance designs before proposing them at work. That is why midPoint is part of the design: access should be requested, approved, recorded and revoked in one place, and the services should only ever see the result. Constraints The directory is authoritative, and Keycloak never writes to it. Account data flows from the directory into Keycloak, never the other way. The university controls its identity provider. The lab's brokers use a registration the university had already issued. The university decides which name-identifier formats it will issue and which attributes it releases, and we cannot change either. Colleagues are external. They authenticate with their university accounts and must not receive directory accounts in order to use a lab service. Configuration is code, and grants are data. Ansible is meant to own realms, clients, identity providers and federation settings; midPoint grants access inside those realms. One operator approves. Every request for a colleague tool that requires approval is reviewed by hand, so the approval path has to be reliable. Design The three products have separate jobs. The directory says who a lab account is. Keycloak proves who is signing in and tells services which groups that person holds. midPoint decides which groups a person should hold, and changes them only through its own policy. sign-in group grants tokens with group claims Directory, university SAML midPoint roles and approvals Keycloak hub realm Lab services Open diagram 1 full size sign-in group grants tokens with group claims Directory, university SAML midPoint roles and approvals Keycloak hub realm Lab services Open diagram 1 full size Diagram 1 Diagram as a table (4 nodes, 0 groups, 3 connections) Node Group Directory, university SAML midPoint roles and approvals Keycloak hub realm Lab services From Link To Relationship Directory, university SAML → Keycloak hub realm sign-in midPoint roles and approvals → Keycloak hub realm group grants Keycloak hub realm → Lab services tokens with group claims Mermaid source flowchart TB Src["Directory,

The lab's default is READ_ONLY , which means Keycloak refuses any change to an imported user. UNSYNCED means Keycloak keeps changes in its own local copy of the user and never writes them to the directory. Realms that broker another identity provider, or that write to the user during sign-in, use UNSYNCED for the directory federation; other realms stay READ_ONLY . The reason is the main failure in this article. The hub realm Since 26 July 2026 the lab has had a hub realm, built so that a person has one account however they arrive. It federates the directory and brokers the university's SAML provider and Google. Newer services sign in at the hub: error tracking, observability, and the lab's documentation site among them. Older application realms predate it and still federate the directory or broker the university themselves, which is why the fix described below had to cover more than one realm. The design's end state is one realm per application, each brokering only to the hub, so that every identity source is configured once. The principle is to authenticate broadly and authorize narrowly: anyone with a lab or university account can prove who they are, and what they can reach is decided by the groups midPoint grants. Brokering the university's SAML provider Keycloak acts as a SAML service provider toward the university under a registration the university had already issued. Keycloak signs its authentication requests. The university signs its responses and encrypts each assertion to the registered certificate, so Keycloak holds that key pair twice, once for signing and once for decryption. We request a persistent name identifier. The university issues it as an opaque, pairwise value, stable for one person at one service provider, which makes it a good link and a poor username. The username therefore comes from an attribute that carries the person's familiar login name. The university does not release a given name for every account type, so a second mapper fills the first name from the display name, which it always releases. Option Why we did not choose it Transient name identifier It changes at every sign-in, so each sign-in would create a new user Username from the name identifier The persistent identifier is an opaque value, unusable as a username Username from the scoped principal name Viable; the shorter login name was preferred Make the first name optional We preferred names that are always populated A separate realm for external collaborators One realm exists only for invited external collaborators. It has no directory federation at all. It brokers the university and Google, and its first-sign-in flow is link-only: a brokered sign-in succeeds only if it matches an account that already exists, and an unmatched identity is rejected rather than registered. The accounts it matches are created by midPoint, disabled until an approval enables them. Governance in midPoint midPoint holds three layers. Each lab application is a service object in its inventory. Each application has its own access roles, and most roles, once assigned, grant a group in Keycloak through midPoint's Keycloak connector. A small set of business roles bundles the combinations people commonly need, such as a baseline for external collaborators, while individual roles remain requestable one at a time. Approval is a reusable metarole. It carries one policy rule: adding an assignment of any role that assigns this metarole opens an approval case with a single stage. Nothing is provisioned while the case is open. The approver is one person, the operator. One role is meant for internal people only. In midPoint 4.9 a role's own policy rule has no selector for the person holding it, so the rule is a global policy rule: it refuses assignment of that role to anyone marked as an external collaborator. approve later A person requests an access role midPoint opens an approval case The approver decides; a rejection provisions nothing midPoint adds the role's group in Keycloak A service that gates on the group admits the person Role unassigned: exactly that group is removed Open diagram 2 full size approve later A person requests an access role midPoint opens an approval case The approver decides; a rejection provisions nothing midPoint adds the role's group in Keycloak A service that gates on the group admits the person Role unassigned: exactly that group is removed Open diagram 2 full size Diagram 2 Diagram as a table (6 nodes, 0 groups, 5 connections) Node Group A person requests an access role midPoint opens an approval case The approver decides; a rejection provisions nothing midPoint adds the role's group in Keycloak A service that gates on the group admits the person Role unassigned: exactly that group is removed From Link To Relationship A person requests an access role → midPoint opens an approval case midPoint opens an approval case → The approver decides; a rejection provisions nothing The approver decides; a rejection provisions nothing → midPoint adds the role's group in Keycloak approve midPoint adds the role's group in Keycloak → A service that gates on the group admits the person A service that gates on the group admits the person ⇢ (dotted) Role unassigned: exactly that group is removed later Mermaid source flowchart TB Req["A person requests

Accounts there belong to the directory federation, to the identity brokers, or to the Keycloak configuration in the repository, so the resource is designed never to create, delete or disable one. The only change it is meant to make is to add or remove the group memberships that hand-assigned roles contribute, and the connector sends each such change with a same-value write of the full user. Two rules make that safe. The first is correlation. midPoint links a hub account to one of its users only when two attributes agree, and never to a system account. Anything less leaves the account unlinked. The second is revocation. Unassigning a role removes exactly the group that role granted. Groups that midPoint did not grant, such as those a broker mapper or the directory supplied, are left in place, and the account itself is kept and stays linked. The configuration behind this is relative assignment enforcement, with the account's existence pinned to true. Why that combination is needed is told below. What went wrong An approval that never fired In June 2026, while codifying midPoint's live configuration into the repository, we found that the approval metarole was not working. Its policy rule sat in an inducement of order two, which applies the rule one level too far down, to the user rather than to the role being assigned. The rule never matched a role assignment, so approval never fired through any channel: the administrative API, self-registration, or a person's own request. We moved the rule to an ordinary order-one inducement, the pattern Evolveum documents for policy metaroles. An end-to-end test then confirmed that an assignment opens an approval case and that nothing reaches Keycloak until the approver approves. The university provider, end to end On 23 July 2026 we pointed the collaborator realm's broker at the university's production Shibboleth service, replacing a local stand-in; the hub, built three days later, brokered the same provider. The configuration was not re-derived for the real provider, and the first end-to-end test, on 27 July, found three latent problems. The provider refused the unspecified name-identifier format we requested. It encrypted assertions to a key Keycloak held only for signing, so decryption failed. And once the format question was settled, the username mapping produced an opaque string. We fixed all three on the hub that day and confirmed a complete sign-in, then codified those fixes and the display-name fallback for both brokering realms and recorded the reasoning in a decision record. The sign-in that failed forever Between 3 and 17 August 2026, brokered university sign-ins failed where the realm also federated the directory in READ_ONLY mode. The person saw a generic error from the identity provider step, and trying again produced the same error. The cause was one unhandled write. Because the lab's brokers force-synchronize profile data, on every brokered sign-in Keycloak compares the email and names in the incoming assertion with the local user and writes back whatever differs. The university supplies the first name from its display name. The directory holds a given name in a different form. For a person with both a directory account and a university account, the two first names differed, so Keycloak tried to set the first name on a read-only federated user. Its federated storage threw a read-only exception, and the throw abandoned the flow before Keycloak saved the link between the university identity and the local account. Nothing was saved, so the next attempt began from exactly the same state and failed the same way. Eleven failures were recorded in those two weeks, and every one was the same write: the first name. Throughout the period, every university sign-in by the operator, who has both kinds of account, failed this way. The fix was to set the directory federation's edit mode to UNSYNCED . The name is easy to misread. UNSYNCED does not give Keycloak write access to the directory. It makes Keycloak's imported copy of the user editable and leaves the directory untouched, which is what the constraint required all along. The same change set two more realms to UNSYNCED . They reach the university through another realm over OIDC, but brokered sign-in runs the same write, and they had not failed only because nobody had brokered into them recently. We also wrote the rule down as a test. As written, it renders the federation configuration from the role's real settings and fails if any realm that federates the directory and brokers an identity provider would come out READ_ONLY . It also fails if a realm with no broker would come out writable, which was meant to keep the fix from widening into blanket write access. The templates render and the linters pass, and the defect exists only at runtime against a live identity provider. The same write without a broker Separately, three days later, the rule turned out to be broader than the one we had written down. A realm with directory federation and no broker at all served an OAuth sign-in whose path writes to the user after a successful password check. A correct directory password produced a bare HTTP 500 with nothing in the server's log and no stored event, while a wrong password was handled normally and a local user signed in without trouble. The realm's event store had been disabled, which is why the failure left no trace. The fix was the same edit mode, and a configuration run confirmed that the provider came out UNSYNCED . Whether a realm brokers was never the real question. The question is whether anything in its sign-in path writes to the user. The revocation that did not revoke In October 2026 the hub resource, as first committed, could not revoke: unassigning a role would not remove its group. We corrected it the same day. The resource had used positive assignment enforcement, chosen so that an unassigned account could never be deleted, and positive enforcement keeps the values a removed role contributed. Relative enforcement removes them, but on its own it turns the loss of an account's last assignment into a decision to delete the account, which skips the group removal and fails against the disabled delete capability. Pinning the account's existence to true resolves both: the account is always meant to exist, and the removed role's group is taken away. A render test checks this configuration, and each of nine deliberate breakages of it makes the test fail. What we learned A read-only store is a property of the directory, not of the sign-in. In April 2026, while first connecting a SAML application to a directory-federated realm, we hit the same read-only exception from a different write: a persistent name-identifier format makes Keycloak store a per-application identifier on the user. We switched that client to send the username as its name identifier, which needs no per-user write. That fixed the instance and left the class in place. Four months later the class came back as a sign-in failure that repeated without end. The general rule is that any realm whose sign-in path writes to the user needs a writable local copy, and UNSYNCED provides one without touching the directory. Guard the invariant, not the instance, and state the invariant precisely. A test written against the real configuration aims to catch the next realm that gains a broker on the workstation instead of in a colleague's browser. It is only as good as the rule it encodes, and our first statement of the rule, keyed on brokers, was narrower than the behavior it was meant to guard against. Test the real path, in both directions. Two of the failures here were invisible until something exercised the whole path: the approval that never fired, and the latent problems with the production university provider. A grant is only tested when both assignment and removal have been watched reaching the service. In midPoint, ownership is not metadata. In July 2026 we routed approvals to each application's owner, so that delegating an application later would mean changing one owner. Owning a role in midPoint also routes approval of changes to that role. Ansible's routine updates to the roles started queuing as approval cases, and the roles could no longer be maintained as code. We reverted to the single fixed approver. Delegation waits until a second owner actually exists. When linking accounts midPoint did not create, correlate narrowly. Linking an account to the wrong person is a security failure. Leaving one unlinked is an inconvenience the operator can resolve by hand. Requiring two attributes to agree keeps the failure on the inconvenient side. Current state Every realm but the external collaborators' realm federates the directory. That federation is READ_ONLY by default and UNSYNCED on every realm that brokers an identity provider or writes to the user during sign-in. The hub realm federates the directory and brokers the university's Shibboleth service and Google. Newer services sign in there, and the remaining application realms are meant to move behind it. midPoint 4.9 holds the application inventory, per-application access roles, business roles, the approval metarole with one approver, and the internal-only assignability rule. Since October 2026 it also governs group membership on the hub through the link-only resource, linking an account only when two attributes agree, and revoking exactly what it granted. References Upstream documentation: Keycloak Server Administration Guide, including LDAP federation edit modes, identity brokering and the first broker login flow: https://www.keycloak.org/docs/latest/server_admin/index.html midPoint 4.9 projection policy and assignment enforcement: https://docs.evolveum.com/midpoint/reference/support-4.9/synchronization/projection-policy/ midPoint 4.9 activation and existence mappings: https://docs.evolveum.com/midpoint/reference/support-4.9/resources/resource-configuration/schema-handling/activation/ midPoint 4.9 policy rules in metaroles: https://docs.evolveum.com/midpoint/reference/support-4.9/roles-policies/metaroles/policy/ midPoint 4.9 policy rules: https://docs.evolveum.com/midpoint/reference/support-4.9/roles-policies/policy-rules/ midPoint 4.9 correlation: https://docs.evolveum.com/midpoint/reference/support-4.9/correlation/ SAML 2.0 core specification, including name identifier formats: https://docs.oasis-open.org/security/saml/v2.0/saml-core-2.0-os.pdf The reasoning here comes from the lab's own architecture decision records, which are not published, chiefly ADR-014 (identity mapping for the university SAML broker against the production Shibboleth provider).

pages.title: Kubernetes on PostgreSQL
pages.summary: Abstract. In May 2026 the lab's Kubernetes control plane could not stay up. Its embedded etcd datastore lived on a virtual disk backed by one SATA hard drive shared with every other virtual machine on the host. Under control-plane load, etcd reported requests taking about thirty seconds, and the control plane restarted roughly every seventy-five seconds. Moving the virtual disks to an iSCSI array, together with turning off a source of heavy watch traffic, ended the crash loop, but under a heavy installation etcd's request durations still peaked at seconds. Our decision record judged that margin too thin to build on, and we replaced etcd with kine, which serves the etcd API from a SQL database, backed by the lab's PostgreSQL server and authenticated with client certificates over mutual TLS. This article tells that chronology from the decision record and from the notes and commits made at the time, describes the design that resulted, and explains what it changed about recovery: restoring the cluster now begins with restoring a database.
pages.text:
This is one article in a series. The overview describes the lab as a whole and the constraints it works under. Context The lab runs one Kubernetes cluster, built with RKE2. In early May 2026 it had a single control-plane node and two workers, all virtual machines on the lab's one Proxmox host. By default RKE2 keeps the cluster's state in etcd, embedded in the control-plane node. etcd is sensitive to storage latency. It commits every change to a write-ahead log and waits for the disk to confirm the write before acknowledging it, and requests queue behind those commits. Leadership is built on top of the datastore. The RKE2 server process runs its own controllers under a leader-election lease held in the datastore, and it must renew that lease before a deadline; when it cannot, the process exits. The controller manager and the scheduler hold leases of their own, but they run as separate pods, and losing one restarts that pod, not the server. A slow datastore therefore becomes a crashing control plane. Our decision record took as working thresholds fsync latency consistently under about 100 milliseconds, with leader elections triggered past about 500 milliseconds. Those figures describe etcd's own Raft elections among several members. Our cluster's etcd had a single member, so the failure we saw ran through the RKE2 server's lease instead. The cluster also had a purpose beyond the lab. We were designing a container platform for university production, which would run on a shared virtualization cluster where the same kind of latency variance is plausible. We wanted its control-plane state in a database that we, and the database administrators we work with, already know how to back up, monitor, recover to a point in time, and eventually make highly available. Constraints The design had to fit the lab as it was, not as we might have wished it to be. One spinning disk under everything. The hypervisor's virtual disks sat on one SATA hard drive, thin-provisioned and shared by more than twenty-five virtual machines. The host has limited room for faster local drives, and adding one would have treated the symptom without changing the design. Network block storage was available. A Synology array already served iSCSI to the hypervisor, so virtual disks could move off the local drive without new hardware. Older silicon. The hypervisor's processor supports the x86-64-v2 instruction set but not v3. PostgreSQL 17 from the vendor's repository would not run on it, so the database server uses PostgreSQL 16 from the distribution, and we build pgBackRest from source. The datastore cannot live inside the cluster it serves. The control plane needs its datastore before it can run anything, so the database has to run outside the cluster. One operator, one database engine. We already run PostgreSQL and expected production to use it. A second database engine would be one more system to patch, back up and understand. Design kine in place of etcd kine is a shim that implements the etcd v3 API on top of a SQL database. RKE2 includes it. When a node's configuration names an external datastore, RKE2 disables embedded etcd and starts kine instead, and every control-plane node points at the same database. There is no etcd cluster initialization and no etcd member join, because the servers hold no datastore of their own. The API server talks to kine as if it were etcd, and kine turns each request into SQL. The effect is to move the storage-sensitive work out of the control plane and into PostgreSQL, a system designed to commit transactions durably and to recover from crashes, and one whose behavior under load we can observe with ordinary database tools. etcd API SQL over mutual TLS, client certificate from the internal CA pgBackRest: WAL archive, full and differential Kubernetes API server control-plane node kine etcd v3 API over SQL PostgreSQL 16 maps certificate names to one database role Off-site object store Backblaze B2 Open diagram 1 full size etcd API SQL over mutual TLS, client certificate from the internal CA pgBackRest: WAL archive, full and differential Kubernetes API server control-plane node kine etcd v3 API over SQL PostgreSQL 16 maps certificate names to one database role Off-site object store Backblaze B2 Open diagram 1 full size Diagram 1 Diagram as a table (4 nodes, 0 groups, 3 connections) Node Group Kubernetes API server control-plane node kine etcd v3 API over SQL PostgreSQL 16 maps certificate names to one database role Off-site object store Backblaze B2 From Link To Relationship Kubernetes API server control-plane node → kine etcd v3 API over SQL etcd API kine etcd v3 API over SQL → PostgreSQL 16 maps certificate names to one database role SQL over mutual TLS, client certificate from the internal CA PostgreSQL 16 maps certificate names to one database role → Off-site object store Backblaze B2 pgBackRest: WAL archive, full and differential Mermaid source flowchart TB API["Kubernetes API server

full and differential"| Archive The database The datastore is a dedicated virtual machine running PostgreSQL 16, with its data on a dedicated virtual disk on the iSCSI-backed storage. The Ansible role that builds it is generic and multi-tenant: a tenant is a role, a database and its access rules, declared as variables. kine was its first tenant. The identity service's database and many cluster applications' databases have joined it since, which is why the overview calls it the lab's shared database. Certificates, not passwords The control plane authenticates to PostgreSQL with mutual TLS. Each control-plane node holds a client certificate issued by the lab's internal certificate authority through the ACME protocol. The certificate's subject is the node's own DNS name, because ACME validates a name by reaching the machine that claims it. PostgreSQL accepts the cluster's connections only over TLS, with certificate authentication, and it maps the certificate's name to a database role through a pattern in its user-name map, so any control-plane node's certificate maps to the same role. No database password exists for this connection. The certificate and its key are readable only by root on the node. Mapping by pattern, instead of creating one database role per node, means a control-plane node can be added or replaced without any change on the database side. That property mattered later in the month. Headroom for leader election On 10 May, during the iSCSI work and the day before the datastore change, we lengthened the leader-election timings of the controller manager and the scheduler from the Kubernetes defaults (a 15-second lease, a 10-second renewal deadline and a 2-second retry period) to 60, 45 and 5 seconds, and they remain in place with kine. A slow datastore response now has to last much longer before either component gives up its lease. The change gives those two components headroom; it does not govern the RKE2 server's own lease. Backups by the database's own tool Because the cluster's state is rows in a PostgreSQL database, it is protected by the same mechanism as every other tenant. pgBackRest archives the write-ahead log continuously and asynchronously, takes a full backup weekly and a differential backup on each of the other six days, keeps two full backups and seven differentials, compresses with zstd, and encrypts on the client with AES-256 before anything leaves the lab. The repository is in Backblaze B2, whose server-side encryption is enabled as well. There is no separate etcd snapshot schedule to maintain, because there is no etcd. Alternatives we rejected Option Why we did not choose it Keep etcd and buy faster disks Limited room for local drives; it treats the symptom, not the cause; it does not match the production environment we were designing for MySQL or MariaDB through kine kine supports both, but we run PostgreSQL and expected production to use it; a second engine adds maintenance for nothing SQLite through kine Gives up any path to high availability; kine's SQLite mode is meant for single-node edge clusters Run the database inside the cluster The control plane needs the database before it can start any workload What went wrong The crash loop on local SATA Under any substantial controller load (a Rancher installation, a cert-manager rollout, even the agents' watch streams), etcd reported single requests taking about 30 seconds. Those were request durations, not disk writes: read requests queued behind consensus commits that were themselves waiting on the disk. On a quiet system the disk answered an fsync in about 4 milliseconds; under sustained writes it took seconds. The RKE2 server could not renew its own lease in time, and it exited with leaderelection lost roughly every 75 seconds, restarted and failed again. Its restart count climbed from zero to 136 within minutes, and the cluster never reached a steady state. We first tried memory, raising the control-plane node from 16 to 24 GB and each worker from 16 to 32 GB. It changed nothing. We also found a second source of load: the watch streams of Cilium's Hubble flow-visibility components were pushing etcd's read times past the RKE2 server's lease deadline. On 10 May we turned Hubble off. iSCSI, and the margin that remained On 10 and 11 May we moved the cluster's virtual disks from the local drive to the iSCSI array. Hubble was turned off in the same two days, so the improvement that followed has more than one cause. The controller-manager and scheduler timings also changed then, but they do not govern the lease whose loss stopped the RKE2 server. etcd's request durations fell from more than 30 seconds to under a second, with readings of about 456 and 503 milliseconds. The crash loop ended: our notes from the time record the three nodes ready and no further restarts. Under the write storm of a Rancher installation, though, request durations still peaked at 4.4 seconds, far above what etcd's guidance expects. The move had its own failure. The disk-move command for the two workers was cut off partway through a script. A cleanup step then removed the disk entries from the virtual machines' configurations, which left nothing to reattach, and the disk files were deleted. Both workers lost their disks. We created empty disks and reinstalled both workers over the network through the provisioning system. Getting them back into the cluster took more than six hours of trial and error. A rejoining node must first be cleared from the control plane, including the password record the control plane keeps for it, and a skipped step fails quietly with a rejected node password or a duplicate node. That session produced a step-by-step reinstall runbook. The other lesson we recorded was narrow and concrete: before removing a disk entry, confirm that the configuration still references a disk that exists. The decision The decision record judged the remaining margin too thin to build on. It names the Rancher installation's load on iSCSI-backed etcd as the trigger, and it puts the iSCSI-backed fsync latency at about 650 milliseconds, roughly six times its own target; that figure is the record's estimate, not a benchmark result. It also had a reason beyond the lab: the production platform we were designing for would face the same kind of latency variance. On 11 May 2026 we moved the cluster's datastore to kine on PostgreSQL. The decision record is dated the same day. After the change, the three nodes reported ready, kine's table was filling, and the RKE2 server had not restarted. The first successful pgBackRest full backup of the new database ran that evening: it took about two minutes and stored 66.8 MB of data as 12.8 MB after compression, and write-ahead log archiving began pushing segments continuously. What we learned Measure the property the failure depends on. Our decision record named fsync latency as the cause without a measurement taken the way etcd's own hardware guidance recommends. On 14 May we added a weekly benchmark modeled on that guidance: small synchronous writes, each followed by a data sync, with the latency percentiles exported to Prometheus. The first run, on the iSCSI-backed virtual machines, made the point. The control-plane virtual machine's 99th percentile was 4.6 milliseconds, but its 99.9th percentile was 202 milliseconds and its worst write took 832 milliseconds. The database virtual machine showed 6.5 milliseconds, 56 milliseconds and 1.27 seconds. The 99th percentile looked healthy. Consensus protocols and lease deadlines feel the tail. Put the sensitivity where it is cheapest to absorb. etcd turns a slow disk into lost leadership and process exits. PostgreSQL turns a slow disk into slow queries, which kine reports as warnings. Neither makes the disk faster, but the second failure mode degrades long before it crashes, and it can be watched with tools we already use. Write down the condition for reversal. The decision record names what would make us undo it: kine's slow-query warnings consistently above two seconds under steady-state load. When we recorded it, those warnings were near zero per hour at idle, with occasional spikes during bursts of reconciliation. The same week, we built a separate test cluster on embedded etcd to check whether the trigger the decision record names, a Rancher installation on iSCSI-backed storage, actually reproduces. No result from it was recorded. The decision therefore rests on the margin argument, not on a reproduced failure, and the stated reversal signal is what lets it be revisited on evidence rather than on mood. Separating the datastore from the control plane made the control plane replaceable. On 25 May we moved the control plane from its virtual machine to a bare-metal server, while the cluster kept running. The new server joined using the shared database, the old node was drained and deleted, and the workers rejoined the new server. Workloads stayed on the workers throughout. Because the database maps any control-plane node's certificate to the same role, the change touched only the cluster's own configuration and none of the database's. The trade-offs are real, and we accept them. There are now two failure domains to keep healthy, the cluster and the database, where there used to be one. Until the database is replicated, it is a single point of failure for the control plane, protected by continuous archiving rather than by redundancy. kine's emulation of the etcd API is not exact, and some rare watch behaviors can differ from etcd's. Current state The lab runs one cluster, and since 25 May 2026 that cluster has hosted Rancher itself. A separate single-node management cluster, which had stayed on embedded etcd, was retired the same day. Rancher, whose installation produced the highest request durations recorded on iSCSI, now runs inside the cluster it manages, and its state is stored through kine in PostgreSQL. The control plane is one bare-metal server. The database and the workers are virtual machines on the hypervisor. If the hypervisor were lost, the control-plane machine would still exist, but the cluster would not run until the database had been restored and the workers reprovisioned. The written restore order reflects this. The database comes back before any Kubernetes work begins, and the restore is checked by confirming that kine's table holds rows. Then the control plane starts and connects to the datastore at boot, the workers rejoin, and Rancher returns with its state already in place. One pgBackRest restore brings back every tenant database on the server, the cluster's included. The recovery point for cluster state is the recovery point of the database: minutes, because the write-ahead log is archived continuously and kine's steady stream of writes keeps segments turning over. A highly available datastore becomes a database change: replacing one PostgreSQL server with a replicated cluster, without re-architecting RKE2. A multi-node control plane remains deliberately deferred. References Upstream documentation: kine, the etcd API over SQL: https://github.com/k3s-io/kine RKE2 external datastores: https://docs.rke2.io/datastore/external etcd hardware recommendations, including disk write latency and benchmarking with fio: https://etcd.io/docs/v3.5/op-guide/hardware/ Kubernetes controller manager flags, including leader-election timings: https://kubernetes.io/docs/reference/command-line-tools-reference/kube-controller-manager/ RKE2 architecture, including which components run as static pods: https://docs.rke2.io/architecture The k3s server's use of leader election, which the RKE2 server inherits: https://github.com/k3s-io/k3s/blob/main/pkg/server/server.go The wrangler leader-election library the k3s server uses, with its lease defaults: https://github.com/rancher/wrangler/blob/main/pkg/leader/leader.go PostgreSQL certificate authentication: https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/auth-cert.html PostgreSQL user name maps: https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/auth-username-maps.html pgBackRest user guide: https://pgbackrest.org/user-guide.html Patroni, for replicated PostgreSQL: https://patroni.readthedocs.io/en/latest/ The reasoning here comes from the lab's own architecture decision records, which are not published: ADR-001 (kine on PostgreSQL instead of embedded etcd), ADR-004 (building pgBackRest from source) and ADR-005 (PostgreSQL 16 from the distribution instead of the vendor's PostgreSQL 17).

pages.title: Secrets in three tiers
pages.summary: Abstract. The lab keeps its secrets in three stores, and our decision record places each secret by one question: does whatever consumes it need it before the runtime secret store is running? Provisioning credentials are encrypted with SOPS and committed to git. A small set of configuration secrets, including the credential Ansible uses to reach Vault, are encrypted with Ansible Vault. Most other secrets, service credentials among them, live in HashiCorp Vault, which keeps its state in cloud object storage and unseals itself through a cloud key-management service. The keys that open the first two tiers, and Vault's own recovery material, are kept in an encrypted break-glass bundle stored outside the lab. This article describes that design and what auto-unseal changes about Vault's recovery keys: they authorize a small set of privileged operations, but they cannot unseal Vault or decrypt its data. It then tells four failures, each since corrected in the code, in which a recovery path looked present but was not: a TLS certificate that expired with nothing to renew it, a break-glass password file that no bundle had ever contained, a helper that the bundle did not carry, and recovery keys that were stored only inside the Vault they recover.
pages.text:
This is one article in a series. The overview describes the lab as a whole and the constraints it works under. Context The lab is rebuilt from code. Terraform and a provisioning system create the machines, Ansible configures them, and Helm charts deploy the cluster workloads. Each step needs credentials at a different moment. The provisioning system's API token is needed before any lab service exists. A service's administrator password is needed when Ansible configures that service. A backup key or a client secret is needed whenever a service is deployed, and it should be possible to change it without a commit. Our decision record (ADR-002) concluded that a single secret store cannot serve all three moments. It rejected keeping everything in Vault because rebuilding from nothing would then need Vault running before Ansible could deploy it, while Vault itself is deployed by Ansible. It rejected keeping everything encrypted in git because every rotation would be a commit, and no value could change without touching the repository. The record set out to give each secret the store whose availability matches the moment it is needed, and to make the loss of each store a recoverable event with a known procedure. Constraints One operator. One person provisions, configures and recovers the lab. Any procedure that depends on a second keyholder, or on remembering an undocumented step, is a procedure that fails. No circular dependency during a rebuild. Nothing needed to bring a store back may live only inside that store. Encrypted at rest in the repository. The configuration repository is the source of truth for the lab. Secrets can sit in it only as ciphertext, and the keys that decrypt them never enter it. We run the authority. We did not want a hosted secrets service to be the single source for fundamental operations. The runtime store is software we run, even though its storage and its seal are cloud services. The hypervisor can be lost. The lab runs on one hypervisor, so the runtime store's data and its unseal mechanism have to survive the loss of that hardware. Design The routing rule Our decision record places each secret by one question: does its consumer need it before HashiCorp Vault is up? If yes, it belongs in one of the two git-backed tiers. If no, it belongs in Vault. Tier Store Unlocked by Contents 1. Provisioning SOPS-encrypted YAML beside the Terraform that uses it An age private key on the operator's workstation The provisioning system's API token, the hypervisor's API token, the directory-join password 2. Runtime HashiCorp Vault, key/value version 2 An AppRole login that issues a short-lived token Service administrator and directory credentials, backup and object-storage keys, OpenID Connect client secrets, archive encryption passwords The second tier is smaller than its name suggests. At the end of April 2026 we replaced most per-role Ansible Vault files with lookups into HashiCorp Vault at apply time, so service credentials now live in tier 3, and tier 2 keeps little beyond the credential that reaches Vault. The tiers form a chain. Tier 1 can be opened with nothing but a file on the workstation, so Terraform can run before any lab service exists. Tier 2 holds the credential that opens tier 3. The plugin runs on the operator's workstation, signs in to Vault with the AppRole credential from tier 2, receives a short-lived token, and reads the value. Ansible then renders it into the service's configuration or into a Kubernetes Secret. On the common path, a running service never talks to Vault; each deployment reads from it. This shapes what rotation means. Rotating a runtime secret is a write to Vault followed by a re-run of the role that consumes it. It needs no commit and no change to any encrypted file, which is the property the runtime tier exists to provide. The Ansible Vault password has two paths The Ansible Vault password itself has two ways in. Day to day, a helper fetches it from HashiCorp Vault, so no person or agent is prompted for it. The original helper, which decrypts a GPG-encrypted copy of the password, is kept as the break-glass path, because it is the only one that works with HashiCorp Vault unreachable. During a rebuild that is the likely case, so the restore runbook overrides the default and names the GPG helper explicitly. That arrangement deliberately keeps one secret in two tiers. The decision record names duplication across tiers as its signal that a boundary is wrong. We read that signal as applying to authoritative copies: the GPG-encrypted password is a recovery copy that keeps the Ansible Vault password available when tier 3 is not. HashiCorp Vault with KMS auto-unseal Vault runs as a single container on one infrastructure host. Its storage backend is cloud object storage, and its seal is a cloud key-management service (AWS KMS). Neither lives on the lab's hardware, so losing the host does not lose the data or the seal: a rebuilt server that points at the same storage with the same cloud identity unseals with its data intact. It terminates TLS itself, with a certificate from the lab's internal certificate authority, and it is not published at the lab's public edge. Vault encrypts everything it stores with a key that is itself protected by a root key, and it starts sealed: it cannot read its own data until the root key is available. With the default Shamir seal, operators supply a quorum of unseal-key shares after every restart. With auto-unseal, Vault asks a trusted device or service to decrypt the root key at startup. For us that means a restart, a host reboot, or a certificate reload brings Vault back unsealed with no person involved. That property is what makes it safe to reload Vault automatically when its certificate is renewed, as described below. The trade is a strict dependency. HashiCorp's documentation is direct about it: if the seal mechanism becomes unavailable, Vault cannot be accessed until it is available again, and if the seal key is permanently deleted, the cluster cannot be recovered, even from backups. What recovery keys can and cannot do When Vault is initialized with auto-unseal, it does not hand back unseal keys. It returns recovery keys, split with Shamir's secret sharing. Ours are five shares, and our runbook records a quorum of three. Recovery keys are an authorization mechanism. A quorum of them is what Vault requires for the operations that would otherwise need unseal keys: Generating a new root token , for example when the root token is lost and directory sign-in is unavailable. Rekeying , which can replace either the recovery-key shares or the key behind Vault's barrier. Replacing the recovery-key shares is the rekey target named recovery , which applies only with auto-unseal or a hardware security module; the default target is the barrier key. Seal migration , where recovery keys are supplied when the old seal is an auto seal. They cannot decrypt the root key. If the key-management service is unreachable, or Vault's cloud credentials have been revoked, Vault stays sealed, and no number of recovery keys changes that. If the key is disabled, Vault unseals on its next start after the key is re-enabled. If the key is deleted, the data in object storage is unrecoverable, with or without recovery keys. AWS KMS does not delete a key immediately: it imposes a waiting period of seven to thirty days, during which deletion can be canceled. A key pending deletion cannot be used in any cryptographic operation, so during that period Vault stays sealed on its next start. Canceling the deletion leaves the key disabled, so Vault unseals only after the key is also re-enabled. So recovery keys protect against losing the root token, not against losing the seal. Recovery from a seal failure means restoring access to the key. For that reason the break-glass bundle carries Vault's cloud identity as well as its recovery keys.
