keys"| RK The break-glass bundle A shell script assembles the keys and recovery material that a lost workstation or infrastructure host would otherwise take with it, and encrypts them into one file: the operator's GPG keyring, whose secret keys remain protected by their own GPG passphrases inside the bundle; the SOPS age key, which opens tier 1; both Ansible Vault password helpers, the GPG-encrypted password file, and the credential the day-to-day helper uses; the internal certificate authority's state; Vault's root token and recovery keys; Vault's cloud identity: the credentials and identifiers for its object storage and its KMS key. The script encrypts the archive symmetrically with GPG, using AES-256 and an iterated, salted passphrase derivation, under a passphrase of at least sixteen characters that the operator holds in memory, with a fallback kept separately from the bundle. The procedure keeps copies outside the lab and shreds the local working copy once they are placed and a decryption check has passed. The bundle is deliberately not stored in the lab's off-site object storage, because reaching that storage depends on credentials the bundle holds. A companion script decrypts a bundle into a temporary directory without restoring anything. It imports the GPG keys into a throwaway keyring, checks the age key's format, validates the certificate authority's archive with the same installer a restore uses, in a mode that installs nothing, confirms that the break-glass password file really decrypts, and checks Vault's recovery fields by name without printing any value. When that password file's key is protected by a passphrase and no terminal is available to unlock it, the script reports the file as unverified and exits with a status of its own instead of passing it. Its last line states its limit: a bundle that decrypts is not proof that the credentials inside still work. The procedure calls for rebuilding the bundle after setup, after rotating the GPG, SOPS or certificate-authority keys it carries, and quarterly, and for verifying each new bundle before the old copies are replaced. Alternatives we rejected Option Why we did not choose it Everything in HashiCorp Vault Rebuilding from nothing needs Vault running before Ansible can deploy it Everything in SOPS Every rotation becomes a commit Everything in Ansible Vault The same drawbacks as SOPS, with weaker support for multiple recipients A hosted secrets service as the single source An external dependency for fundamental operations, and authority outside the lab What went wrong Each of these failures has the same shape: a recovery path existed on paper, and something quietly kept it from working. The certificate that nothing renewed Vault was deployed at the end of April 2026. Its Ansible role issued a TLS certificate from the internal certificate authority with a 90-day lifetime, and the task was guarded so that it ran only when no certificate existed. Nothing renewed it. By late July the certificate had expired, silently, and every client that reached Vault over TLS failed: the workstation's session helper, Ansible, and the deployments that read from it. On 29 July we added a daily systemd timer, with jitter and catch-up after downtime. It checks whether fewer than thirty days remain, issues a fresh certificate if so, and reloads Vault. We chose a fresh issuance over a renewal because it produces a fixed lifetime every time and still works if the certificate has already expired, which a renewal refuses. The reload recreates the container, and that is safe only because of auto-unseal: Vault comes back unsealed with nobody present. A break-glass path that no bundle had ever contained The first bundle script, written in May, captured the GPG-based Ansible Vault helper and was meant to capture the encrypted password file it decrypts. It found that file by searching the helper's text with a pattern that expected a path beginning with a slash. The helper wrote the path relative to the home directory, so the match produced a path that did not exist, the existence check failed, and the script printed a mild note and moved on. On 2 August we found that the file had almost certainly never been in any bundle. Every bundle contained the break-glass helper but not the encrypted password it needs, so the path that was supposed to work with the lab down could not have worked at all. The fix expands the home-directory forms, and the message now names the path it looked for and states the consequence. A helper the bundle did not carry The same day, we made the Vault-backed helper the default for Ansible Vault. The GPG helper depended on a passphrase cache that was wiped whenever the GPG agent restarted, and each restart surfaced as a password failure. The change introduced a second gap: the bundle carried only the GPG path, so a restore would have produced an Ansible configuration naming a helper that was not there. The same fix captures both helpers and the credential the new one needs. The restore runbook gained a warning at the top. With Vault down, the default fails, and the failure looks like a wrong password rather than an outage, which is a hard thing to diagnose in the middle of a recovery. Recovery keys stored inside the Vault they recover When Vault was initialized, its root token and recovery keys were stored in Vault itself. Auto-unseal never asks for them, but it also means they can be read only while Vault is healthy. In the scenarios where they matter most, such as a lost host, a seal problem, or a lost root token with directory sign-in down, they were out of reach. On 8 October we extended the bundle to export the root token, the recovery keys and Vault's cloud identity, printing only field names as it goes. The verification script now checks those fields by name. What we learned A recovery path is not real until something checks it. All four failures were silent. A certificate was valid until it was not, a script printed a gentle note instead of failing, and a configuration change left the bundle a step behind the workstation. A missing file now produces a warning that names the file and the consequence. The verification script checks Vault's recovery fields by name and says plainly that decrypting is not recovering. And the certificate is renewed by a timer instead of by memory. Auto-unseal moves the risk; it does not remove it. It removed a person from every restart, and it is what makes reloading Vault after a certificate renewal safe. In exchange, the lab's ability to read its own secrets depends on one key in a cloud service. Recovery keys do not hedge that dependency. Access to the key does, and the bundle carries Vault's cloud identity for that reason. Convenience paths and recovery paths should be different paths. The Vault-backed helper is the right default for unattended work. It is also the path most likely to fail during the disaster it would be needed for. Keeping the GPG path, and saying in the script and the runbook why it must not be tidied away, preserves the property the tiers were designed for. The decision record's question applies to recovery material too. It was not asked of Vault's own root token and recovery keys until October, although their consumer, by definition, needs them when Vault is not available. Current state The three tiers are as described above. Tier 1 holds provisioning credentials encrypted with an age key. Tier 2 holds Ansible's credential for Vault and a few host credentials under an Ansible Vault password that reaches Ansible through HashiCorp Vault day to day, or through GPG when Vault is down. Tier 3 is configured as HashiCorp Vault 1.18.4, auto-unsealed by a cloud KMS key, with its storage in cloud object storage, read by Ansible through an AppRole that issues short-lived tokens. Vault's TLS certificate is configured with a 90-day lifetime and set to be reissued automatically once fewer than thirty days remain. The bundle script captures both Ansible Vault paths, the internal certificate authority's state, and Vault's root token, recovery keys and cloud identity, and its companion checks Vault's recovery fields by name. A bundle is only as current as the last time the script ran, which is why the procedure calls for rebuilding it after rotating the GPG, SOPS or certificate-authority keys, and quarterly. References Upstream documentation: HashiCorp Vault seals, auto-unseal and recovery keys: https://developer.hashicorp.com/vault/docs/concepts/seal HashiCorp Vault AWS KMS seal configuration: https://developer.hashicorp.com/vault/docs/configuration/seal/awskms HashiCorp Vault operator generate-root : https://developer.hashicorp.com/vault/docs/commands/operator/generate-root HashiCorp Vault operator rekey : https://developer.hashicorp.com/vault/docs/commands/operator/rekey HashiCorp Vault AppRole authentication: https://developer.hashicorp.com/vault/docs/auth/approle AWS KMS key deletion and its waiting period: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/kms/latest/developerguide/deleting-keys.html SOPS: https://github.com/getsops/sops age: https://github.com/FiloSottile/age Ansible Vault: https://docs.ansible.com/ansible/latest/vault_guide/index.html smallstep step certificate needs-renewal : https://smallstep.com/docs/step-cli/reference/certificate/needs-renewal/ The reasoning here comes from the lab's own architecture decision records, which are not published: ADR-002 (three-tier secrets) and ADR-001 (kine on PostgreSQL), which shows a secret turned into certificate distribution instead.
